newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnians face gas cuts due to debt dispute.
newsitem.headline: Bosnians face gas cuts due to debt dispute.

text.p: Bosnians who suffered without heating during 43 months of war must now endure more cuts in gas supplies due to a dispute over a debt owed to Russian suppliers, a Western official said on Tuesday.
"As of eight o'clock yesterday morning, the Russian suppliers started reducing the gas supplies into Bosnia-Herzegovnina," Tony James of the Overseas Development Administration (ODA) told reporters.
James said the reduction amounted to a 40 percent cut in the natural gas supply for a country which relies heavily on gas for winter heating.

Unseasonably warm weather this week had postponed the effects of the cutbacks for the moment, James said. "When the temperature turns and the temperature will turn quite suddenly then you will feel the full impact."
Gas is already rationed in the capital Sarajevo, with heating cut off intermittently according to a reduction schedule.
For Sarajevans, the gas cuts bring back terrible memories of the 3-1/2 year siege of their city, when heating and power were cut off amid relentless Serb shelling attacks.
James said the Russian "Gas Export" company cut back gas deliveries because Bosnia has failed to pay a $12.4 million debt covering a six-month period dating back to October 1995.

Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic have been arguing for months about the share of the debt each territory owes, said James, who has overseen international efforts to resolve the dispute.
Both sides refuse to take financial responsibility for heating to Sarajevo suburbs which were being transferred from Serb control to the federation last winter.
The federation says it lacked full administrative power over the city districts during the transfer of authority.

The Bosnian Serbs have agreed to pay $3.5 million of the total debt and the federation has agreed to pay $3.6 million. But the two sides still appear no closer to agreeing who should pay the remaining amount, James said.
"That leaves $5.25 million which is hanging in the air...I believe the international community could pick it up because otherwise we will be arguing about it for the next 50 years."
Federation and Serb prime ministers were due to meet this week in an attempt to end the deadlock, he said.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) expressed concern that the gas reductions would hurt the most vulnerable in Bosnia, especially thousands of impoverished elderly Sarajevans who receive daily meals at soup kitchens.
Some of the kitchens rely on natural gas and will have to shut down because of the cuts, said Nina Winquist-Galbe, a spokeswoman for the ICRC.
